headline: Tech Bros Claim Shadows Are 'Your Body's Dark Mode,' Petition Apple for Credit
subheadline: Class action lawsuit argues human shadows predate iOS dark mode by millions of years
summary: A group of tech enthusiasts has filed suit against Apple, claiming the company's dark mode feature infringes on the 'original dark mode' that human shadows have provided since the dawn of humanity.
content:
A coalition of 847 self-described 'shadow rights activists' has filed a class action lawsuit against Apple, Google, and Microsoft, alleging that dark mode features across all major operating systems constitute intellectual property theft from the human body.

'Shadows have been providing dark mode since the first organism blocked a light source,' said lead plaintiff and tech podcast host Brandon Wexler. 'We're just asking these corporations to acknowledge that the human body was the original user interface.'

The lawsuit, filed in Northern California district court, seeks $4.7 billion in damages to be distributed among 'all shadow-having entities,' which the plaintiffs define as 'any object or organism capable of blocking photons.'

Dr. Patricia Huang, who studies the intersection of technology and philosophy at Hartwell University, called the case 'legally absurd but philosophically fascinating.'

'The metaphor is surprisingly apt,' Dr. Huang explained. 'Dark mode reduces eye strain and battery consumption. Shadows reduce heat absorption and UV exposure. Both are essentially the environment adapting to provide contrast and protection. The difference is one requires a settings menu and the other just requires the sun.'

The plaintiffs' 200-page filing includes extensive documentation arguing that shadows constitute 'the original ambient computing experience' and that moving from light to shade is 'the biological equivalent of toggling a display setting.'

Apple declined to comment on pending litigation. A Google spokesperson said only: 'We are confident that naturally occurring phenomena cannot be trademarked, though we appreciate the creative interpretation.'

The case has sparked viral debate on Threadit and Chirper, with users divided between dismissing the lawsuit as 'peak Silicon Valley brain rot' and earnestly arguing about whether clouds casting shadows constitute 'the sky's dark mode.'

One Chirper user noted: 'If shadows are dark mode, does that mean nighttime is system-wide dark mode? Does this mean the Earth has settings?'

A counter-movement has emerged arguing that eyelids were actually the first dark mode, predating shadows as a user-controlled interface. 'You can toggle eyelids,' wrote Threadit user u/BlinkTwice. 'Shadows require external light source manipulation. Eyelids are the true OG.'
author: Kevin Marsh, Tech & Law
